articles.title: How to Run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next FP4 Locally (It Needs Blackwell and 55 Env Vars)
articles.summary: NVIDIA's FP4 build of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next is 96 GiB on disk. The BF16 original is about 355 GB. NVIDIA says the accuracy cost of that shrink is 0.7 points on GPQA Diamond. If you want to run Qwen3.8 Flash Next locally, that sounds like the obvious download. It isn't, at least not yet. The first line of the model card tells you upstream vLLM can't load it. Blackwell is the only supported architecture, and the RTX PRO 6000 launch script exports 55 environment variables before it gets to vllm serve. This post covers what NVIDIA changed, how the size stacks up against GGUF, which benchmark numbers hold up, and the run commands for RTX PRO 6000 and DGX Spark. My sources are the NVIDIA model card, the Qwen card, Unsloth's and bartowski's GGUF pages, and the community speed thread. I haven't run this checkpoint myself, so every number here comes from those pages, linked inline. What NVIDIA actually changed The base model is Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, released on August 26, 2026 (Qwen blog).

articles.title: Black Forest Labs' open-weights image model FLUX 3 Image Klein runs on consumer GPUs with just 8 GB of VRAM
articles.summary: Black Forest Labs has released FLUX 3 Image Klein, a 5.6-billion-parameter open-weights image model that supports native 4K generation, pixel-precise editing, and generation with up to ten reference images. With 38 percent fewer parameters than its predecessor, it still outperforms proprietary competitors in internal tests and runs on GPUs with just 8 GB of VRAM. The article Black Forest Labs' open-weights image model FLUX 3 Image Klein runs on consumer GPUs with just 8 GB of VRAM appeared first on The Decoder.

articles.title: Gen4P: Video Generators are 4D Perceivers
articles.summary: We introduce Gen4P, a unified framework for recovering 4D geometry and motion from monocular video. We show that a pretrained video generator can be repurposed into a feed-forward 4D perceiver without iterative denoising. Building on on-demand querying, Gen4P processes clean video latents in a single encoder pass and predicts the requested 4D attributes through a lightweight cross-attention decoder. The on-demand query formulation enables flexible spatial sampling, and our proposed continuous-time queries further provide temporal flexibility. To strengthen geometric knowledge, we propose a straightforward plug-in solution by incorporating a pretrained video-depth LoRA as a frozen geometry prior, improving overall performance without adding extra trainable parameters. Gen4P achieves state-of-the-art or competitive performance on tasks of 3D point tracking, video depth and camera pose estimation. articles.title: GeoState: Learning View-Decoupled Geometry States for 3D World Modeling
articles.summary: Recent 3D world models increasingly use features from geometry foundation models (GFMs) as predictive world states, benefiting from their rich geometric priors. However, the view dependence of these features entangles scene dynamics with camera-induced variation, making the resulting state evolution harder to predict. We propose GeoState, a view-decoupled geometry representation for predictive 3D world modeling that separates scene-state evolution from camera-dependent observation. Specifically, a scene tokenizer aggregates multi-view GFM features into a view-decoupled scene state, which a geometry decoder queries using camera rays. An autoregressive world model then predicts future scene states, while camera motion is modeled separately. The predicted states can therefore be decoded under either predicted or externally specified cameras, while retaining a single context-derived scale throughout the rollout without per-frame scale alignment. articles.title: Denoising Textures is a Different Ballgame Altogether!
articles.summary: The human brain effortlessly deciphers colors and textures from visual stimuli and reconstructs the world around us, yet preserving such details remains challenging in image denoising. While significant progress has been made in generic image denoising, the problem of texture denoising has remained relatively under-explored. Fine details, such as intricate patterns and repetitive structures, often suffer from over-smoothing even in deep learning based approaches for denoising. In this paper, we analyze the behavior of state-of-the-art (SOTA) denoisers on texture datasets and show that performance improvements are possible only by fine-tuning the denoisers on the texture datasets. Surprisingly, fine-tuning on texture datasets result in the models catastrophically forgetting the original dataset. articles.title: 44 days of AI signals as a dataset — and 3 silent API traps I hit publishing it
articles.summary: I've been collecting AI signals from public sources every day for 44 days. This week I published the whole thing as a machine-readable dataset. Along the way I hit three failure modes that were completely silent — no error, no log line, just "nothing happens". They're worth knowing if you publish a public API or dataset, because they cost me hours and I'd rather you skip them.
